## Functions

### `createRealmLifecycleParticipantAuthority(options)`

Genuine per-host participant delivery, not lifecyclePort@1 or a full provider. Exact frozen options { identityAuthority } require the genuine private source. Output is exactly frozen { registerParticipant, hostLifecycle, close }. Registration consumes the existing mutable exact eight-field adapter request and synchronously returns frozen { participantId, dispose }. One genuine owner binding can issue one participant across sources; repeats with identical roots and callbacks share its handle, while disposed owners cannot register again. hostLifecycle is the v3 synchronous acceptance source, not the wrapped channel. It keeps the latest suspension and first terminal cause in constant space. At most one suspension invocation and one terminal invocation are queued per participant. Ordinary delivery requires real current owner/work authority; terminal delivery uses the originally authenticated retained owner after work abort or operator invalidation. No caller label or generic event is authority. Callbacks are captured with their original receiver, invoked later with zero arguments, and must synchronously return undefined (as the existing adapter does). Returned promises/thenables never become cleanup dependencies. Fixed warnings report rejected callbacks without leaking their payloads. Acceptance proves enqueueing, never callback success, Entry stop or renderer suspension. dispose() fences synchronously and awaits only owned invocation settlement; close() refuses an undisposed participant or unsettled disposal. Neither retires owners, aborts roots, waits for Entry, or drives resource cleanup. The original issuer's operator-change subscription is notification-only and cannot make OperatorContext wait for Realm teardown. Trusted construction and host intrinsics are required; no isolated acquisition or recovery is claimed.

## Notes & Examples

### Command Bus Pattern

The OS uses a capability-gated command bus for inter-app and system communication. Apps register command handlers; the kernel routes commands based on capabilities. Commands can be local (same app), cross-app (with permission), or system-level (elevated).

**Example: Command registration and invocation**
```js
import { CommandBus } from 'webgpu-os/kernel/CommandBus.js';
import { Capability } from 'webgpu-os/kernel/Capability.js';

const bus = new CommandBus();

// Register a handler (requires 'ui' capability)
bus.register('myapp:openFile', async (path) => {
  const content = await storage.read(path);
  return { content, size: content.length };
}, { capability: 'storage' });

// Invoke locally
const result = await bus.invoke('myapp:openFile', '/docs/readme.md');

// Cross-app invocation (requires 'interop' capability)
const otherApp = bus.proxy('otherapp');
const data = await otherApp.invoke('otherapp:compute', input);

// Broadcast to all listening apps
bus.broadcast('system:themeChanged', { theme: 'dark' });
```

**See also:** [WebGPU OS Architecture](/webgpu-os/architecture.md) · [Security Model](/concepts/security-model.md)
